      I agree, he is a great & patient teacher. I wish I had a teacher like that in school...since I was really bad at English. Unfortunately I didn't find any video yet, that taught me something new. I taught myself English by watching movies & series with English Subtitle, every day, many hours...years over years.
      I can read English extremely fast because of it. I don't even say the words in my head, I just look at the sentences briefly (like talking a picture of the whole sentence) & I understand. I learned grammar, vocabulary etc without actually learning. 
      The fun part was, that the movies/series themselves weren't in English, they were another foreign language (e.g. Japanese, Korean, Chinese) which I learned with reading the English Subtitle. So, I was able to learn 2 foreign languages at once. Very effective for lazy people haha.
      I took a couple of years, but now I can understand e.g. Japanese 95%, when watching movies/series & don't even need any Subtitle anymore. 
      So, I can recommend doing that. Of course to put the reading & the pronunciation together, watching movies/series which are actually in English should be added. But I never used Subtitles for that...but for people who have problems, it's surely useful.

  When I was learning German 🇩🇪, it took me some time to build the confidence to read a book. I was trying to read magazine articles very early. They were a bit easier in that they were shorter and I could choose to try to read something I liked and had some knowledge about already. The tabloid style 📰 were best because they generally do not use complex language. I could even work my way through "professional" material because they were shorter and focused 🔎 on a particular subject matter. 
  
  Later I picked up a Young Adult novel 📖. It was challenging at first. I started out looking up words, then marking them for later 🖍. After a while, I decided just to bulldoze my way though 🚧 because it was to much effort to keep interrupting the process. I found that as I continued, I understood more by virtue of exposing myself to the material. I could infer definitions by context and was so excited when I finished! 🎉

  I think I read a lot faster than most other people, even faster than average native English speakers. But I think this bad habit, reading fast, messed up my English. First off, I read fast because I want to get the contents of the books asap, which made me lazy looking up the dictionaries for correct pronunciation. I catch the meaning s of new words in the context of the text or passage instead of looking up for proper pronunciation.
  
  Also, I have to read the same book several times for I miss a lot at first or second round of reading.
  
  Reading fast helps to catch the overall contents of the books fast and efficient. But when it comes to scientific and technical subject matter, it only slows down and hinders my concrete and solid understanding. 
  
  I always advise my son to read slow, but diligently.
  
  Reading slow is not slow. It saves me tremendous time and frustrations. I always whisper to myself, "Tom, read slow, if you don't want to read it again!"

**@focuslee1343** (👍0 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J622HQz79QY&lc=UgwYn9rDcnNf6BfSvwJ4AaABAg
  - "creature of habit". If you say that someone is a creature of habit, you mean that they usually do the same thing at the same time each day, rather than doing new and different things.
   - "break a habit". It means end , stop the habit. 
   - "force of habit". If you do something from force of habit, you do it because you have always done it in the past, rather than because you have thought carefully about it. 
   - "fall back into". It means that to go back to doing something or behaving in a way which you did before.
   - "old habits die hard". It means that it is difficult to end a habit.
   - "kick a/the habit". It means that end a habit or to give up something harmful taht you have done for a long time .
   - "break the habit". It is the same meaning of kick the habit.
   - "have an/the urge".

**@voltronsupremeFood** (👍9 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gBEpjL_J7OU&lc=UgwbnbYNYwxLP2BOe_V4AaABAg
  I frequently rag on James, but I have to admit he does a many  things that will help you with  your conversations.  First notice he dresses well, So one thing to take is that you want to bring your best self forward.  He is dress dapper.  Two he is wearing a bow, while traditionally people-wear is a tie,  a bow can be used as an ice breaker in a conversation. It  helps other open up to you by acting as a conversation piece. Thirds thing is the empathy, instead of just saying aaahh you can invite them continue talking by asking them questions.  The fourth thing that James does is hand gestures.  The gestures are not over powering and flow with his tone of voice and hence make the conversation more lively.  Five knowing how to subtlety change your voices tone.   I do disagree on one point is the use of "OK" or "And"   because tone of voice is crucial, if you say ok with the wrong tone it can come off as sarcastic.  If you are unsure if your tone for OK is sarcastic or leading, then it better to not use OK and follow up with a positive leading question.   Follow these sets and you will come off as charismatic.  Remember too smile subtlety too, Like James does in his videos.  Compare James to the others on engvid notice that the others are uncharismatic and one could easily argue  extremely dull.

    ↳ **@werds1392** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qrYRDCty9y8&lc=Ugzu9Dk4yeYv6uCBwfB4AaABAg.8gL7tT2fLix8hW285YzSHX
      João Matamba Quimuanga basically wonder means to think about something. You could say, “I wonder what is going to happen tomorrow” or “I wonder what she is going to say.” Wander, on the other hand, means to walk around aimlessly or to leave the path you are supposed to be on. A runner who is competing in a race might “wander” off of the track, and that would probably cause the crowd to “wonder” what is wrong with him.  
      Edit: just a little extra information. Wander (as in walk around without a destination in mind) would be a good word to use if somebody is walking around a mall without knowing what store they want to go into.

      Lutch Bizin in general, “checking something out” sometimes implies that the person doing the checking has never seen that thing before. When I load up my email, I usually say that I am checking it because I am familiar with my email account. If my friend tells me about a song I’ve never heard before I might respond, “okay, I’ll go check it out” before I go listen to it. 
      With all that said it’s important to stress that this is not a rule, it’s just something that can provide a guide in most situations.

  Mine is more of a commentary on the larger implications of American English. It is exactly the reason British English sounds infinitely more elegant - especially Received Pronunciation. In my opinion, new comers to the English language ought to, at least during the incipient stages of apprehending American English, understand the contractions that the language is replete with - like gonna, sorta, etc. I am actually fascinated that new learners of English are able to understand American English. British English by contrast is sympathetic to how the language is written, at least in the main. I speak and write Italian. Italians say of their language: Come si scrive, si legge. This simply translates: The way it's written is the way it's spoken. Good luck trying that with the English language. By the way, praises for your infusion of levity, jest and relaxed humor.
  - Godfrey Silas

**@juanfran579** (👍0 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6pxUmP82aQw&lc=UgxSsFdFcP2vWfKC-XZ4AaABAg
  Strangely enough, I've come to the stage as a learner and teacher of English as a second language to make a distinction between sounding and speaking like a native speaker. Sounding like a native speaker means to me to get to a good standard pronunciation, being capable of modulating your voice naturally ( relaxed speaking ), making use of a wide range of vocabulary and , of course, showing a good command of grammar aspects as they come up in natural speech. Nevertheless, neither am I aiming at speaking like a native speaker nor am I pushing my students to do so. I mean it's up to you to take up a rather posh RP,  Glaswegian, Texas dialect or whatever standard or adaptation or not. I'd give my students the advice to keep sticking to what they identify with instead of turning into someone else. Ist's perfectly alright to speak good standard, no matter whether it's based on British, American or whatever guideline.

  Conjunctions like for, so because, and or are easy everyday words used to join words, clauses and phrases together.
  
  Correlative conjunctions join statements of related information.
  
  
  
  either or (choice)
  
  not only  but also(surprise)
  
  neither nor( negation)
  
  both and (including)
  
  
  
  
  
  conjunction pairs
  
  neither you nor you hairy-assed friend can come to my party.
  
  
  
  Conjunction examples
  
  
  
  1.They told me to either buy the shoes or put them back.(choice)
  
  2. Not only did it smell, but it also tasted funny.(surprise)
  
  3. The dog either ate nor slept that night(negation)
  
  4. Mr E. was both funny and modest about his adventures.(including)
  
  
  
  
  
  1, quizzes
  
  
  
  a.__2_ inclusion
  
  b.__4_ choice
  
  c.__3_ negation
  
  d.__1_ surprise
  
  
  
  1. Not only was it of great quality, but it was also cheap.
  
  2. Both the man and his dog were stupid.
  
  3. neither the woman nor the man were happy with the answer.
  
  4. Either you watch the program or we turn off the television.

    ↳ **@Vampsailormoon** (👍3 · 2026-08-08) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CwcmwkEoMcU&lc=UgxjAnoV79mDY-O2Y5Z4AaABAg.A_A_icRy6lwA_CJjuoySWV
      not everything you consume has to be high art. tastes are varied. every book is going to have haters and fans. 
      I think learning to be okay with listening to criticism of books you like can help you to better understand your own tastes and develop a deeper relationship with books you read. sometimes the criticisms are valid. 
      like maybe the plot of a certain book really is silly and vapid. you can decide that, despite the fact that that might bothers other readers, it doesn’t bother you. You can acknowledge that it’s true, without having the same opinion about it as other people. I find that super helpful for when I’m reading reviews and deciding on whether I should read a certain book or not. If the one big problem most reviewers have with the book is something that I’ve learned doesn’t bother me, then that’s a good sign that I’ll like the book! 
      On the other hand, sometimes valid criticisms include pointing out something morally wrong that the author has done or written. that’s the kind of situation where, if you want to keep reading their book, you make sure not to spend your money in a way that would benefit the author, and apply a more critical lense to reading that author’s work from now on.
      
      there’s nothing wrong with you for enjoying things others might deem unenjoyable or “low quality”

  Lights everywhere, people laughing and bickering. Jaipur was indeed glowing as diwali was coming. In one of the crowded lanes, right in the middle of all this celebration, a girl was running, laughing about something.
  "Oh no, no, no. Why can't you run a little faster? Mr. Mishra will kill us if we're late again today!" she said, stopping for a second and turning back.
  Behind her, a girl stood far away, bent over and panting. She pushed her glasses back up to the bridge of her nose. "Oi, double battery, run faster!" the first girl shouted.
  "You can't be serious with me, Kiara," the girl with the glasses replied between breaths. "How can we be late again,bro?"
  Kiara made a skeptical face. "Well, can't blame you. All that studying at night is finally showing off."
  With that, both girls started running again.
  Kiara kept glancing back at Ruhi, laughing, and didn't notice where she was going. She suddenly bumped into someone hard. "Oh shi— sorry," Kiara blurted out.
  When she looked up, she was met with what felt like a soft wall of falling flowers. A basket had tipped over, petals spilling everywhere between them.
  She wanted to stop and apologize properly, but Ruhi grabbed her arm and pulled her forward."C'mon, we're getting late," Ruhi said urgently.
  "Sorry!" Kiara called out over her shoulder as they ran away.
  They reached the school just in time to see the guard closing the gate.Ruhi turned to Kiara, half terrified and half curious. "Kiara, we are so done."
  "Not so fast. Follow me," Kiara said, already moving.
  She ran to the other side and threw her bag over the wall.
  "Kiara, are we really doing this again? It's the third time this month," Ruhi said, glaring at the wall as her mind raced.
  "You got a better plan, huh?" Kiara asked.
  Ruhi shook her head. "Then follow me, smartass," Kiara said.
  Kiara jumped over the wall, with Ruhi right behind her. They grabbed their bags and sprinted to their classroom.
  Their professor, Mr. Mishra—a man in his mid-forties with round glasses and a very large forehead now lined with anger—was already standing inside."Oh, look, students," he said dryly. "Our great pupils, Ms. Kiara and Ms. Ruhi, have finally arrived. Mind telling us what got you so late, ladies?"
  Ruhi opened her mouth, unsure whether to apologize or make an excuse, but Kiara jumped in."Sir, we were on time, but—"
  Mr. Mishra raised an eyebrow. "But what, Kiara? Did a dog chase you, or did you both forget the way to school?"
  Ruhi's face went pale, but Kiara, sharp as ever, replied, "No, sir. A kid was stuck on a tree, asking for help. We helped him and got late."
  Mr. Mishra crossed his arms. "Oh, what a nice deed. What was the child's name, ladies? Tell me at the same time."
  Ruhi looked at Kiara, half terrified. Kiara pretended to stutter, giving her a hint. "Sir... that kid had a name something like b... b..."
  Ruhi took a breath, as if she'd understood—or decided to pretend she had.
  "Bunty!" Kiara blurted out."Ballu!" Ruhi said at the exact same time.
  The classroom fell silent. For a moment, neither of them moved. Then a few students burst into laughter.
  Ruhi slowly turned toward Kiara. Kiara slowly turned toward Ruhi.
  Mr. Mishra removed his glasses and pinched the bridge of his nose."Remarkable," he said. "Absolutely remarkable."
  The laughter only grew louder.
  "Not only are you late," Mr. Mishra continued, putting his glasses back on, "but you couldn't even agree on the name of the child you so heroically rescued."
  Ruhi opened her mouth, but Kiara beat her to it."Sir, actually—"
  
  "Enough, Kiara." She immediately shut her mouth.
  
  Mr. Mishra pointed toward the door."Both of you. Outside. For the entire period."
  Ruhi's face dropped. Kiara let out a dramatic sigh. "Sir, don't you think that's a little harsh for two brave citizens who saved a child?"
  Mr. Mishra raised an eyebrow. "Would you like me to make it detention as well?
  "Kiara straightened instantly. "No, sir."
  "Good. Outside."
  The moment the classroom door closed behind them, Ruhi rounded on Kiara. "Bunty?
  "Kiara looked at her as if she'd said something outrageous. "What do you mean, Bunty? You said Ballu!"
  Ruhi threw her hands in the air. "Because I thought you were saying Ballu!". 
  Kiara pointed accusingly at her. "I was clearly saying Bunty!"
  "You were stuttering!" Ruhi shot back.
  "I was giving a hint!"
  "It was a terrible hint!"
  Kiara scoffed. "Still better than Ballu."
  Ruhi gasped dramatically. "What's wrong with Ballu?"
  "Everything."
  Ruhi smacked her lightly on the shoulder.
  Kiara pouted dramatically as if Ruhi had done the ultimate betrayal to her."Ow! Violence! Now I
  know why Mr. Mishra punished us."
  "Shut up."Despite herself, Ruhi started laughing. A second later, Kiara joined in.
  From inside the classroom, Mr. Mishra's voice echoed through the door."I can still hear both of you."
  
  The laughter stopped immediately.A pause.Then the girls looked at each other. And burst out laughing again.

      This fear is not unfounded--and it's very good to be wary of AI tools that make big promises just to steal your work--but there are nuances. Never upload your paper to any platform unless you are on a paid plan that provides data privacy. E.g. The major American LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) , as far as I know, don't train their models on your files/chats if you're on the paid tiers. If you're using a free tool/free plan, then that tool is absolutely taking your data for their commercial use in some form or fashion. I think the fear of someone wholesale taking your paper and publishing it in a journal is unlikely, but you still don't want an LLM feeding on your work. Even if you're on a paid platform, double check their policies about how they handle your data.

One thing from my native perspective, btw: "prevailing wisdom" is a bit formal sounding, like something you'd read in a school essay and some newspaper articles. It's correct and good to know, but if you want to use something a little less formal and more everyday you might also choose any of the following: accepted belief, conventional wisdom, traditional wisdom, popular opinion, general consensus, widespread view, etc. All of these sound a bit more modern and commonplace to my ears. **@Kei-p2u-e3s** (👍50 · 2025-11-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MZ0r2dcAqM4&lc=UgxpsRPEWKANBRpkKDl4AaABAg
  In this video, she talked about the Japanese tadoku method (extensive reading).
   I’m Japanese, and I have read a book about the Japanese tadoku method, so I would like to share my ideas based on the book.
  As she said, the point of the Japanese tadoku method is to focus on the amount of reading passages rather than reading intensive books.
   The merit of this strategy is that we can gain more reading experience and encounter words that were new to us.
   As a result, our vocabulary expands more quickly.
  In addition, this method has another advantage.
   It allows us to acquire the building blocks to think more deeply about various ideas.
   This is not only related to language learning but also useful for thinking in general, as well as for thinking more academically or about complex matters.
   This is because if we accumulate more and more ideas and vocabulary, weeks or even years later, that knowledge can become the spark for a new idea.
  The author of the book I read called this process “zyousei.”
   “Zyousei” means “cultivation” in English.
  I think this is very helpful for learning languages.
   For example, the knowledge I acquired a few years ago can suddenly become active vocabulary, allowing me to understand certain words’ meanings or nuances more deeply.
  Considering the above reasons, I think the Japanese tadoku method is extremely effective for language learning!

  I want to learn English mainly through listening, while keeping my original accent when I speak. My goal is simply to make my speech as clear as possible.
  
  I am a bit confused about which content to focus on. In the UK, there are so many regional accents, many of them very difficult to understand, and even some British people struggle with each other’s accents. The BBC accent isn’t really spoken by people in everyday life, and if I try to use it myself, I feel it might sound strange.
  
  In the US, I know there are also many accents, but it seems that most people speak General American — whether in news broadcasts, TV shows, movies, or in public life. Even if there are other American accents, they are usually quite close to General American and easy to follow. Also, American content is much more abundant — countless series, films, podcasts, and television programs — compared to British content.
  
  So, what do you think? My only purpose in learning English is to communicate with people all around the world, including in America, Britain, and everywhere else. English is a global language, a bridge that connects you with the rest of the world.
  
  Thank you all for your thoughts.-)

  I know one more rule:
  FISH / FISHES
  
  Fish = same kind or food
  Example: We ate fish. I caught two fish.
  
  Fishes = different species
  Example: The aquarium has many fishes.
  
  
  FRUIT / FRUITS
  
  Fruit = general meaning or same kind
  Example: I like fruit. / She bought some fruit.
  
  Fruits = different types of fruit
  Example: The market sells tropical fruits.

   𝙎𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙛𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙎𝙖𝙣𝙨 𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙖𝙘𝙡𝙚
  
  (𝓣𝓪𝓷𝓴𝓪, 𝓗𝓪𝓲𝓴𝓾, 𝓣𝓪𝓷𝓴𝓪 & 𝓗𝓪𝓲𝓴𝓾)
  
  
  An anonymous
  
  Helping hand feels twice too grand;
  
  Being vincible
  
  And much too invisible
  
  To feel deeply lovable.
  
  
  In dark, secret hours
  
  Whispering a sincere prayer
  
  Is the highest care.
  
  
  Be off the self-scoff :
  
  Satisfaction sans show off
  
  Is real self-care
  
  Happiness' receptacle
  
  Is content sans spectacle.
  
  
  The joy of giving
  
  Without telling it in text
  
  Makes one God —the next.
